questions.question_text:
Each process P_i, i = 1...9 is coded as follows:
repeat
  P(mutex)
  {critical section}
  V(mutex)
forever
The code for P_10 is identical except that it uses V(mutex) in place of P(mutex). What is the largest number of processes that can be inside the critical section at any moment?

options.label: D
options.text: None of these

questions.explanation: Every time process P_10 enters, it performs a V (UP) operation instead of a P (down) operation, so after that one more process can enter the critical section. This phenomenon continues, allowing up to 10 processes at a time to be inside the critical section, so none of the given options (1, 2, or 3) is correct.

questions.explanation: Initial value is 10. Six P (down) operations reduce it by 6 to 4, and four V (up) operations increase it by 4, giving 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.question_text:
Two concurrent processes P1 and P2 use four shared resources R1, R2, R3 and R4, as shown below:
P1: Compute; Use R1; Use R2; Use R3; Use R4;
P2: Compute; Use R1; Use R2; Use R3; Use R4;
Both processes are started at the same time, and each resource can be accessed by only one process at a time. The following scheduling constraints exist between the access of resources by the processes:
- P2 must complete use of R1 before P1 gets access to R1.
- P1 must complete use of R2 before P2 gets access to R2.
- P2 must complete use of R3 before P1 gets access to R3.
- P1 must complete use of R4 before P2 gets access to R4.
There are no other scheduling constraints between the processes. If only binary semaphores are used to enforce the above scheduling constraints, what is the minimum number of binary semaphores needed?
questions.explanation: With only one semaphore the constraints cannot all be enforced since binary semaphores allow only a single wait/signal pair; trying with two binary semaphores a and b shows all four constraints can be satisfied, so the minimum number needed is 2.

questions.question_text:
Synchronization in the classical readers and writers problem can be achieved through use of semaphores. In the following incomplete code for readers-writers problem, two binary semaphores mutex and wrt are used to obtain synchronization
wait (wrt)
writing is performed
signal (wrt)

wait (mutex)
readcount = readcount + 1
if readcount = 1 then S1
S2
reading is performed
S3
readcount = readcount - 1
if readcount = 0 then S4
Signal (mutex)
The values of S1, S2, S3, S4, (in that order) are

options.label: A
options.text: signal (mutex), wait (wrt), signal (wrt), wait (mutex)

options.label: B
options.text: signal (wrt), signal (mutex), wait (mutex), wait (wrt)

options.label: C
options.text: wait (wrt), signal (mutex), wait (mutex), signal (wrt)

options.label: D
options.text: signal (mutex), wait (mutex), signal (mutex), wait (mutex)

questions.explanation: The first reader must lock out writers (S1 = wait(wrt)), then release mutex to let other readers in (S2 = signal(mutex)); before decrementing readcount at the end a reader must reacquire mutex (S3 = wait(mutex)), and the last reader leaving must release the writer lock (S4 = signal(wrt)), matching option (c).

questions.question_text: Three concurrent processes X, Y and Z execute three different code segments that access and update certain shared variables. Process X executes the P operation (i.e., wait) on semaphores a, b and c; process Y executes the P operation on semaphores b, c and d; process Z executes the P operation on semaphores c, d and a before entering the respective code segments. After completing the execution of its code segments, each process invokes the V operation (i.e., signal) on its three semaphores. All semaphores are binary semaphores initialized to one. Which one of the following represents a deadlock-free order of invoking the P operations by the processes?

options.label: A
options.text: X: P(a)P(b)P(c), Y: P(b)P(c)P(d), Z: P(c)P(d)P(a)

options.label: B
options.text: X: P(b)P(a)P(c), Y: P(b)P(c)P(d), Z: P(a)P(c)P(d)

options.label: C
options.text: X: P(b)P(a)P(c), Y: P(c)P(b)P(d), Z: P(a)P(c)P(d)

options.label: D
options.text: X: P(a)P(b)P(c), Y: P(b)P(c)P(d), Z: P(c)P(d)P(a)

questions.explanation: Tracing each option line by line for all three processes shows that only option (b) avoids a cycle in the wait-for graph among X, Y and Z, so it is the only deadlock-free order.

questions.question_text: A shared variable x, initialized to zero, is operated on by four concurrent processes W, X, Y, Z as follows. Each of the processes W and X reads x from memory, increments by one, stores it to memory, and then terminates. Each of the processes Y and Z reads x from memory, decrements by two, stores it to memory and then terminates. Each process before reading x invokes the P operation (i.e., wait) on a counting semaphore S and invokes the V operation (i.e., signal) on the semaphore S after storing x to memory. Semaphore S is initialized to two. What is the maximum possible value of x after all processes complete execution?
questions.explanation: With S initialized to 2, two processes can read x concurrently before either stores it back. By carefully interleaving the reads and writes of W, X, Y, and Z (allowing lost updates), the maximum final value of x that can be achieved is 2.

questions.question_text: Consider a non-negative counting semaphore S. The operation P(S) decrements S, and V(S) increments S. During an execution, 20 P(S) operations and 12 V(S) operations are issued in some order. The largest initial value of S for which at least one P(S) operation will remain blocked is ____.
questions.explanation: With initial value S, after 20 P and 12 V operations the net change is S - 20 + 12 = S - 8; for at least one P operation to remain blocked, this final value must be negative, i.e., S - 8 < 0, giving the largest integer value S = 7.

questions.question_text: A multithreaded program P executes with x number of threads and uses y number of locks for ensuring mutual exclusion while operating on shared memory locations. All locks in the program are non-reentrant, i.e., if a thread holds a lock l, then it cannot re-acquire lock l without releasing it. If a thread is unable to acquire a lock, it blocks until the lock becomes available. The minimum value of x and the minimum value of y together for which execution of P can result in a deadlock are:
questions.explanation: Since locks are non-reentrant, a single thread trying to re-acquire the same lock it already holds without releasing it will block itself forever, so a deadlock can occur with just one thread and one lock, i.e., x = 1, y = 1.

questions.question_text:
Consider three concurrent processes P1, P2 and P3 as shown below, which access a shared variable D that has been initialized to 100.
P1: D = D + 20
P2: D = D - 50
P3: D = D + 10
The processes are executed on a uniprocessor system running a time-shared operating system. If the minimum and maximum possible values of D after the three processes have completed execution are X and Y respectively, then the value of Y - X is ____.
questions.explanation: The minimum value occurs when P1 and P3 read D before P2 updates it: P1 and P3 both read D = 100 and later write 110 and 120 respectively, and P2's update of 50 applies last, giving D = 100 - 50 = 50 = X. The maximum occurs when P2 and P3 read the initial value and update sequentially, then P1 reads the updated value: giving D = 110 + 20 = 130 = Y. Hence Y - X = 130 - 50 = 80.

questions.question_text: Consider the following snapshot of a system running n concurrent processes. Process i is holding X_i instances of a resource R, 1 <= i <= n. Assume that all instances of R are currently in use. Further, for all i, process i can place a request for at most Y_i additional instances of R while holding the X_i instances it already has. Of the n processes, there are exactly two processes p and q such that Y_p = Y_q = 0. Which one of the following conditions guarantees that no other process apart from p and q can complete execution?

options.label: A
options.text: X_p + X_q < Min {Y_k | 1 <= k <= n, k != p, k != q}

options.label: B
options.text: Min (X_p, X_q) >= Min {Y_k | 1 <= k <= n, k != p, k != q}

options.label: C
options.text: Min (X_p, X_q) <= Max {Y_k | 1 <= k <= n, k != p, k != q}

options.label: D
options.text: X_p + X_q < Max {Y_k | 1 <= k <= n, k != p, k != q}

questions.explanation: Since p and q request no more resources, they can complete and release their X_p and X_q instances, making X_p + X_q instances available. For no other process to be able to complete, this available amount must be less than the smallest additional request among all remaining processes, i.e., X_p + X_q < Min {Y_k | k != p, q}.

concepts: Barrier-style synchronization using count and semaphores

options.label: A
options.text: It ensures that at most two processes are in CODE SECTION Q at any time.

options.label: B
options.text: It ensures that all processes execute CODE SECTION P mutually exclusively.

options.label: C
options.text: It ensures that no process executes CODE SECTION Q before every process has finished CODE SECTION P.

options.label: D

questions.explanation: All processes remain blocked on wait(b) until count reaches n, at which point b becomes 1, allowing a process into CODE SECTION Q; hence no process can enter CODE SECTION Q until all n processes have finished CODE SECTION P.

options.label: B
options.text: The value of counter is 0 after all the threads successfully complete the execution of parop.

options.label: C
options.text: There is a deadlock involving all the threads.

options.label: D
options.text: The value of counter is 5 after all the threads successfully complete the execution of parop.

questions.explanation: If threads interleave the non-atomic counter++ operation, a lost update can make the final counter value 1. If all five threads perform both wait(S) operations first (using up all 5 permits), none can proceed further, causing a deadlock. If instead the threads execute the whole function sequentially without interleaving the increment, counter correctly ends at 5. A final value of 0 is not possible given the interleavings.

questions.question_text:
Consider a computer system with multiple shared resource types, with one instance per resource type. Each instance can be owned by only one process at a time. Owning and freeing of resources are done by holding a global lock (L). The following scheme is used to own a resource instance:
function OwnResource (Resource R)
  Acquire lock L // a global lock
  if R is available then
    Acquire R
    Release lock L
  else
    if R is owned by another process P then
      Terminate P, after releasing all resources owned by P
      Acquire R
      Restart P
      Release lock L
    end if
  end if
end function
Which of the following choice(s) about the above scheme is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The scheme violates the mutual exclusion property.

options.label: B
options.text: The scheme ensures that deadlocks will not occur.

options.label: C
options.text: The scheme may lead to live-lock.

options.label: D
options.text: The scheme may lead to starvation.

questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion is not violated since ownership is always exclusive. Deadlocks cannot occur because a process's resources are forcefully preempted (by terminating it) rather than being held indefinitely. However, if processes keep repeatedly preempting each other's resources, this can lead to starvation of some processes and a live-lock where processes keep restarting without making progress.

options.label: D
options.text: At least one of the threads will print the value of y as 2.

questions.explanation: Since x and L1 are global variables within each process's own address space (not shared across processes), each process's two threads increment their own copy of x from 0 to 2, so both P1 and P2 print x as 2. Since y is a local variable in foo(), each thread has its own separate copy of y, so every thread always prints y as 1, never 2.

To get the sequence starting with B, only S1 must be initialized to 1 (allowing T2 to run first and print B), while S2 and S3 must both start at 0 so T3 and T1 remain blocked until signaled in the correct order.

questions.question_text:
Consider the two functions incr and decr shown below:
incr() { wait(s); X = X + 1; signal(s); }
decr() { wait(s); X = X - 1; signal(s); }
There are 5 threads each invoking incr once, and 3 threads each invoking decr once, on the same shared variable X. The initial value of X is 10. Suppose there are two implementations of the semaphore s, as follows:
I-1: s is a binary semaphore initialized to 1.
I-2: s is a counting semaphore initialized to 2.
Let V1, V2 be the values of X at the end of execution of all the threads with implementations I-1, I-2, respectively. Which one of the following choices corresponds to the minimum possible values of V1, V2, respectively?
concepts: Binary vs counting semaphore critical section access
questions.explanation: With a binary semaphore (I-1), only one thread can be in the critical section at a time, so incr and decr always execute correctly one at a time; the only possible final value of X is 12, so V1's minimum is 12. With a counting semaphore of value 2 (I-2), two threads can access the critical section concurrently, allowing a maximum number of decrements' effects to be preserved and increments' effects to be lost through races, giving a minimum possible V2 of 7.

Each iteration of the loop doubles the number of active processes through fork(), and each active process executes the printf statement once per iteration it participates in; summing the number of printf executions across the three iterations of the loop for the original process and all its descendants gives a total of 14.

concepts: Binary semaphore trace across three processes
questions.explanation: Since A is initialized to 1, only one process can be inside the section up to X = X+1 at a time, so a third '*' cannot be printed before the '$' appears (which happens exactly when the second process increments X to 2); this rules out option (d), while options (a), (b) and (c) are all achievable through valid interleavings of the three processes.
